title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges.

nearMiss.why: Union-Find can group overlaps, but checking all pairs is O(n²); sorting by start makes it one sweep.
Choosing a maximum set of non-overlapping intervals is greedy by end; merging is a sweep by start.
A heap helps when counting concurrent intervals (rooms); merging needs only the last merged interval.

trigger.why: Overlap / merge on [start, end] pairs ⇒ sort by start, compare with the last merged end.

ds.answer: int[][] sorted by start (Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0])) + List<int[]> result
wrong: TreeMap<Integer, Integer> start → end without sorting logic
ds.why: After sorting, only the last merged interval can overlap the next one. A boolean[] per point blows up with large coordinates.

invariant.answer: After processing interval i, the result is the merged form of intervals 0..i, and only its last entry can still grow.
wrong: The result is sorted by end time.
Every interval is compared with every earlier interval.
The last merged interval never changes once added.
invariant.why: Sorted starts mean a new interval either extends the last one or begins a gap.

wrong: Union-Find only works on sorted data.
Union-Find would merge non-overlapping intervals too.

approach: Sort by start. For each interval: if it starts after the last merged end, append it; otherwise extend the last end to max(lastEnd, end).

title: Insert Interval
statement: Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start and a new interval, insert it so the list stays sorted and non-overlapping, merging where necessary.

nearMiss.why: Binary search finds where to insert in O(log n), but merging and copying the output is O(n) anyway.
The list is already sorted; a heap adds O(n log n) for nothing.
There is no pair to converge on; it's a single left-to-right sweep in three phases.

trigger.why: Interval overlap + already sorted ⇒ one sweep: copy before, merge overlapping, copy after.

ds.answer: List<int[]> result built in one pass, with an index into the input
wrong: int[] coverage array over the coordinate range
ds.why: The input is sorted; no extra structure is needed.

invariant.answer: Intervals ending before the new start are copied as-is; every interval overlapping the new one is folded into it; the rest are copied after.
wrong: The new interval is always appended at the end.
Only the first overlapping interval is merged.
The output may contain overlaps that a second pass removes.
invariant.why: Three phases in order keep the output sorted and disjoint.

wrong: Binary search can't work on intervals.
Binary search needs the intervals unsorted.
Binary search would merge every interval.

approach: Copy intervals with end < newStart. While interval start ≤ newEnd, newStart = min, newEnd = max. Add the new interval, then copy the rest.

title: Meeting Rooms II
statement: Given meeting time intervals [start, end], return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that no two meetings in the same room overlap.

nearMiss.why: Choosing which meetings to keep is greedy by end; here every meeting must be held, so you count overlaps.
Grouping overlapping meetings doesn't give the peak number happening at once.
There is no choice to optimise; the answer is the maximum overlap depth.

wrong: no two meetings in the same room overlap
trigger.why: Max number of intervals overlapping at once ⇒ sort starts and ends (sweep line) or a min-heap of end times.

ds.answer: Intervals sorted by start + PriorityQueue<Integer> min-heap of end times (or two sorted arrays of starts and ends)
ds.why: The heap's size is the number of rooms in use; its root is the earliest room to free up.

invariant.answer: The heap holds the end times of meetings still running at the current start time.
wrong: The heap holds every meeting ever scheduled.
The heap is ordered by start time.
invariant.why: Before each start, pop the root if it has ended; the max heap size is the answer.

space.why: The heap in the worst case (all overlap).

wrong: Greedy only works with one room.
Greedy would need the meetings to be non-overlapping.

approach: Sort by start. For each meeting: if the heap's earliest end ≤ start, poll it; offer this end. Answer = max heap size (= final size with this variant).

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement: Given intervals [start, end], return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove so that the remaining intervals do not overlap.

nearMiss.why: A DP over sorted intervals works in O(n²) (or n log n with binary search), but the earliest-end greedy is simpler and optimal.
Counting concurrent intervals with a heap answers 'how many rooms', not 'how few removals'.
Trying every subset to remove is exponential.

trigger.answer: minimum number of intervals you need to remove
trigger.why: Fewest removals = keep the most non-overlapping intervals ⇒ classic interval scheduling: greedy by earliest end.

ds.answer: int[][] sorted by END (Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[1])) and one int lastEnd
wrong: int[][] sorted by start with a merge list
ds.why: Sorting by end is the crux; sorting by start needs extra care to pick which to drop.

invariant.answer: lastEnd is the end of the last kept interval, which is the earliest possible end for that many kept intervals.
wrong: lastEnd is the largest end seen so far.
Intervals are kept in order of their start.
Every interval longer than the average is removed.
invariant.why: Ending earliest leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument).

time.why: The sort; the sweep is linear.

wrong: DP would give the maximum removals instead.
DP needs the intervals to be disjoint already.

approach: Sort by end. Keep a count of kept intervals and lastEnd; if start ≥ lastEnd keep it (lastEnd = end), else remove it. Answer = n − kept.

title: Jump Game
statement: You start at index 0 of an array where each value is your maximum jump length from that position. Return true if you can reach the last index.

nearMiss.why: BFS over every jump works but can be O(n²) edges; tracking the farthest reach is O(n).
Trying every jump sequence is exponential.
There's no window property; the only state is how far you can reach.

trigger.why: Reachability where every position up to the farthest reach is also reachable ⇒ one greedy variable: farthest.

ds.answer: One int: farthest index reachable so far
wrong: boolean[] reachable table updated for every jump
ds.why: Reachable positions form a prefix, so its end is all you need.

invariant.answer: Every index ≤ farthest is reachable; if i > farthest you are stuck.
wrong: farthest is always the last index.
You always jump the maximum length.
farthest only increases when nums[i] is the largest seen.
invariant.why: Extending farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]) keeps the prefix property.

wrong: BFS would need the jumps sorted.
BFS only works when all jumps are 1.

approach: farthest = 0; for i: if i > farthest return false; farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]). Return true.

twists.change: From index i you jump to exactly i + nums[i] or i − nums[i], and the goal is any index holding 0.
twists.statement: Start at index start. From index i you may jump to exactly i + nums[i] or i − nums[i] (staying in bounds). Decide whether you can reach any index whose value is 0.
twists.ds: ArrayDeque<Integer> queue (or recursion) and boolean[] visited

nearMiss.why: The 'farthest reach' trick needs jumps of ANY length up to nums[i] in one direction; exact two-way jumps break it.
Jumps go both ways, so there's no order to fill a table in.
Nothing converges; it's reachability in an implicit graph.

twists.why: Each index has two outgoing edges ⇒ BFS/DFS with a visited set.
twists.approach: BFS from start; if nums[i] == 0 return true; enqueue unvisited in-bounds i ± nums[i]. Return false.

title: Task Scheduler
statement: Given CPU tasks labelled A–Z and a cooldown n, identical tasks must be at least n intervals apart (idle slots allowed). Return the minimum number of intervals needed to finish all tasks.

nearMiss.why: The cooldown looks like a window, but you're constructing a schedule, not scanning a given sequence.
No subproblem recurrence is needed; the most frequent task dictates the frame.
There are no dependencies between different tasks, only spacing between identical ones.

trigger.why: The most frequent task forces (maxCount − 1) frames of length n + 1; greedily fill gaps with others (or simulate with a max-heap).

ds.answer: int[26] counts (formula) or PriorityQueue<Integer> max-heap of counts with a cooldown queue
ds.why: Only counts matter, not task identities or order.

invariant.answer: Scheduling the most frequent remaining task first never makes the total longer.
wrong: Idle slots are inserted after every task.
The answer is always the number of tasks.

time.answer: O(T) with the formula (T = number of tasks)

wrong: A window would need the tasks sorted.
Sliding window only works when n = 0.

approach: Count tasks; maxCount = top count; ties = number of tasks with that count. Answer = max(tasks.length, (maxCount − 1) × (n + 1) + ties).

title: Meeting Rooms
statement: Given an array of meeting time intervals [start, end], decide whether one person could attend all of them, i.e. whether any two meetings overlap.

nearMiss.why: A min-heap of end times counts rooms (Meeting Rooms II); for a yes/no overlap check, sorting and comparing neighbours is enough.
Hashing exact times can't detect partial overlaps.
There is no selection to optimise: every meeting must be attended, so it's purely an overlap check.

wrong: an array of meeting time intervals
trigger.why: Overlap between intervals ⇒ sort by start and compare each with the previous end.

ds.answer: int[][] sorted with Arrays.sort(a, Comparator.comparingInt(x -> x[0]))
ds.why: After sorting, only neighbours can overlap first.

invariant.answer: After sorting by start, if no meeting starts before the previous one ends, no pair overlaps at all.
wrong: Meetings are sorted by end time.
Each meeting overlaps at most one other.
The earliest meeting is also the shortest.
invariant.why: A later meeting starts even later, so checking adjacent pairs is sufficient.

wrong: A heap would return the longest meeting.

approach: Sort by start; for i ≥ 1 if a[i][0] < a[i − 1][1] return false. Return true.

title: Interval List Intersections
statement: You are given two lists of closed intervals; each list is pairwise disjoint and sorted. Return the intersection of the two lists: every overlap between an interval from the first and one from the second.

nearMiss.why: With two lists, two indices are enough; a heap adds nothing.
Binary-searching each interval in the other list is O(n log m) and still has to walk overlaps.
There's nothing to rank; both lists are already in order.

trigger.answer: every overlap between an interval from the first and one from the second
trigger.why: Two sorted interval lists ⇒ walk both: overlap = [max starts, min ends]; advance whichever ends first.

ds.answer: Two int indices i, j and List<int[]> result
ds.why: Already sorted: no sort, no heap.

invariant.answer: All intersections involving intervals before i (in A) or before j (in B) are already recorded; the interval that ends first can't overlap anything further.
wrong: i and j always advance together.
The result is built in reverse order.
invariant.why: lo = max(starts), hi = min(ends); if lo ≤ hi record it.

wrong: A heap can't store closed intervals.
k-way merge needs at least three lists to be correct.
k-way merge would union the intervals instead.

approach: While i < A.length and j < B.length: lo = max(A[i][0], B[j][0]); hi = min(A[i][1], B[j][1]); if lo ≤ hi add [lo, hi]; advance the one with the smaller end.

title: Gas Station
statement: Stations on a circular route give gas[i] fuel, and driving from station i to i + 1 costs cost[i]. Starting with an empty tank, return the index of the station from which you can complete the full circuit, or -1. If a solution exists it is unique.

nearMiss.why: Net-gain prefix sums are part of the reasoning (start after the lowest point), but the single-pass reset rule is the whole algorithm.
It resembles a running sum that resets, but the goal is a feasible start, not a maximum-sum subarray.
Simulating from every start is O(n²); no DP state is needed once you see the reset argument.

trigger.why: If the tank goes negative between start and i, no station in that stretch can be the start ⇒ reset the start to i + 1 (greedy).

invariant.answer: tank is the fuel accumulated from start to i; when it goes negative, every station from start to i is ruled out as a starting point.
wrong: The answer is the station with the most gas.
total and tank are always equal.
Prefix sums can't handle circular arrays.
Prefix sums need sorted gas values.
Prefix sums would give the farthest station reachable.

approach: For i: diff = gas[i] − cost[i]; total += diff; tank += diff; if tank < 0 { start = i + 1; tank = 0; }. Return total ≥ 0 ? start : -1.

title: Jump Game II
statement: From index i you can jump forward up to nums[i] steps. Starting at index 0, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index (it is always reachable).

nearMiss.why: dp[i] = min jumps works but is O(n²) in the worst case; the greedy level-by-level reach is O(n).
Every edge costs 1, so Dijkstra is overkill; it's an implicit BFS, done greedily with two scalars.
The 'window' is a BFS level, not a contiguous range with a sum or budget.

wrong: jump forward up to nums[i] steps
trigger.why: Fewest jumps = BFS levels over indices; the greedy version tracks the current level's end and the farthest next reach.

ds.why: The BFS frontier is a contiguous range, so two ints describe it.

invariant.answer: All indices ≤ currentEnd are reachable in `jumps` jumps; farthest is how far one more jump can get from them.
wrong: currentEnd only increases by 1 each step.
invariant.why: At i == currentEnd: jumps++, currentEnd = farthest.

wrong: DP would only say whether the end is reachable.

approach: For i in 0..n−2: farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]); if i == currentEnd { jumps++; currentEnd = farthest; }. Return jumps.

title: Partition Labels
statement: Split a string of lowercase letters into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. Return the sizes of the parts in order.

nearMiss.why: The part's end is pushed by each letter's LAST occurrence, not by a count budget; you never shrink from the left.
Merging overlapping letter spans with DSU works but is heavy; one pass with last positions is enough.
No choices need comparing: the earliest valid cut is always the best.

trigger.answer: each letter appears in at most one part
trigger.why: Each letter spans [first, last]; parts are merged spans ⇒ record last positions, extend the current end, cut when i reaches it.

ds.answer: int[26] last index of each letter, plus scalars start and end

invariant.answer: end is the furthest last-occurrence of any letter seen in the current part; when i == end, no letter in the part appears later.
wrong: Each part contains distinct letters only.
end only moves when a new letter appears.
invariant.why: Cutting as early as possible maximises the number of parts.

wrong: A sliding window would give the fewest parts.
Sliding windows need the string sorted.

approach: last[c] = final index of c. For i: end = max(end, last[s[i]]); if i == end, add end − start + 1, start = i + 1.
